`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`[§](https://docs.rs#comparing-fixed-point-numbers)Comparing fixed-point numbers

With floating-point numbers like [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), checking two numbers for equality can
require calculating both the absolute difference
(|

*a*−

*b*|) and the relative difference (|

*a*−

*b*| /

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements conversions and comparisons with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

# fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fixed/1.31.0/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/fixed/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fixed-point-numbers)Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An *n*-bit fixed-point number has
*f* = `Frac`
fractional bits where
0 ≤ *f* ≤ *n*,
and
*n* − *f*
integer bits. For example, [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U24.html)>*n* = 32
total bits,
*f* = 24
fractional bits, and
*n* − *f* = 8
integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
*Δ* = 1/2 f.
When

*f*= 0, like in

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*Δ*= 1 because representable numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When

*f*=

*n*,

*Δ*= 1/2

and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤

*n**x*< 0.5 for signed numbers like

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>*x*< 1 for unsigned numbers like

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12::from_num(19) / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!(six_and_third.to_string(), "6.3333");
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil().to_num::<i32>(), 7);
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil(), 7);
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U12](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U12.html)>[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I4F12};
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4::from_num(1);
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!(ans1, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 3));
assert_eq!(ans1.to_string(), "3.2");
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12::from(a);
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4::from_num(wider_ans);
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!(ans2, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 6));
assert_eq!(ans2.to_string(), "3.4");
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fixed-point-numbers)Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An *n*-bit fixed-point number has
*f* = `Frac`
fractional bits where
0 ≤ *f* ≤ *n*,
and
*n* − *f*
integer bits. For example, [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U24.html)>*n* = 32
total bits,
*f* = 24
fractional bits, and
*n* − *f* = 8
integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
*Δ* = 1/2 f.
When

*f*= 0, like in

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*Δ*= 1 because representable numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When

*f*=

*Δ*= 1/2

and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12::from_num(19) / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!(six_and_third.to_string(), "6.3333");
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil().to_num::<i32>(), 7);
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil(), 7);
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U12](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U12.html)>[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I4F12};
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4::from_num(1);
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!(ans1, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 3));
assert_eq!(ans1.to_string(), "3.2");
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12::from(a);
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4::from_num(wider_ans);
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!(ans2, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 6));
assert_eq!(ans2.to_string(), "3.4");
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`[§](https://docs.rs#comparing-fixed-point-numbers)Comparing fixed-point numbers

With floating-point numbers like [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), checking two numbers for equality can
require calculating both the absolute difference
(|

*a*−

*b*|) and the relative difference (|

*a*−

*b*| /

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements conversions and comparisons with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-optional-features)Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::- [f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::- [bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements conversions and comparisons with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-optional-features)Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::- [f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::- [bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)

[524](#524)macro_rules! fixed {
[525](#525)    (
[526](#526)        description = $description:literal,
[527](#527)        {Self, Inner} = {$Self:ident, $Inner:ident},
[528](#528)        Signedness = $Signedness:ident,
[529](#529)        LeEqU = $LeEqU:ident,
[530](#530)        {Unm1, Un} = {$Unm1:ident, $Un:ident},
[531](#531)        [nm4 ..= np1]
[532](#532)            = [$nm4:literal, $nm3:literal, $nm2:literal, $nm1:literal, $n:literal, $np1:literal],
[533](#533)        {ISelf, IInner} = {$ISelf:ident, $IInner:ident},
[534](#534)        {USelf, UInner} = {$USelf:ident, $UInner:ident},
[535](#535)        [LeEqUC0 ..= LeEqUC3] = [$LeEqUC0:ident, $LeEqUC1:ident, $LeEqUC2:ident, $LeEqUC3:ident],
[536](#536)        nbytes = $nbytes:literal,
[537](#537)        {bytes_val, rev_bytes_val} = {$bytes_val:literal, $rev_bytes_val:literal $(,)?},
[538](#538)        {be_bytes, le_bytes} = {$be_bytes:literal, $le_bytes:literal $(,)?},
[539](#539)        $(
[540](#540)            n2 = $n2:literal,
[541](#541)            {Double, DoubleInner} = {$Double:ident, $DoubleInner:ident},
[542](#542)            {IDouble, IDoubleInner} = {$IDouble:ident, $IDoubleInner:ident},
[543](#543)        )?
[544](#544)    ) => {
[545](#545)        comment! {
[546](#546)            $description, "-bit ",
[547](#547)            if_signed_unsigned!($Signedness, "signed", "unsigned"),
[548](#548)            " number with `Frac` fractional bits.
[549](#549)
[550](#550)The number has ", $n, " bits, of which <i>f</i> = `Frac` are
[551](#551)fractional bits and ", $n, " − <i>f</i> are integer bits.
[552](#552)The value <i>x</i> can lie in the range ",
[553](#553)            if_signed_unsigned!(
[554](#554)                $Signedness,
[555](#555)                concat!("−2<sup>", $nm1, "</sup>/2<sup><i>f</i></sup>"),
[556](#556)                "0",
[557](#557)            ),
[558](#558)            " ≤ <i>x</i> < 2<sup>",
[559](#559)            if_signed_unsigned!($Signedness, $nm1, $n),
[560](#560)            "</sup>/2<sup><i>f</i></sup>. The difference between successive
[561](#561)numbers is constant throughout the range: <i>Δ</i> = 1/2<sup><i>f</i></sup>.
[562](#562)
[563](#563)For <code>", stringify!($Self), "\\<[U0]></code>, <i>f</i> = 0 and
[564](#564)<i>Δ</i> = 1, and the fixed-point number behaves like ",
[565](#565)            if_signed_unsigned!($Signedness, "an", "a"),
[566](#566)            " [`", stringify!($Inner), "`] with the value lying in the range ",
[567](#567)            if_signed_unsigned!(
[568](#568)                $Signedness,
[569](#569)                concat!("−2<sup>", $nm1, "</sup>"),
[570](#570)                "0",
[571](#571)            ),
[572](#572)            " ≤ <i>x</i> < 2<sup>",
[573](#573)            if_signed_unsigned!($Signedness, $nm1, $n),
[574](#574)            "</sup>. For <code>", stringify!($Self), "\\<[U", $n, "]></code>,
[575](#575)<i>f</i> = ", $n, " and
[576](#576)<i>Δ</i> = 1/2<sup>", $n, "</sup>, and the value lies in the
[577](#577)range ",
[578](#578)            if_signed_unsigned!(
[579](#579)                $Signedness,
[580](#580)                "−1/2 ≤ <i>x</i> < 1/2",
[581](#581)                "0 ≤ <i>x</i> < 1",
[582](#582)            ),
[583](#583)            ".
[584](#584)
[585](#585)`Frac` is an [`Unsigned`] as provided by the [*typenum* crate].
[586](#586)
[587](#587)`", stringify!($Self), "<Frac>` has the same size, alignment and ABI as
[588](#588)[`", stringify!($Inner), "`]; it is `#[repr(transparent)]` with
[589](#589)[`", stringify!($Inner), "`] as the only non-zero-sized field.
[590](#590)
[591](#591)# Examples
[592](#592)
[593](#593)```rust
[594](#594)use fixed::types::extra::U3;
[595](#595)use fixed::", stringify!($Self), ";
[596](#596)let eleven = ", stringify!($Self), "::<U3>::from_num(11);
[597](#597)assert_eq!(eleven, ", stringify!($Self), "::<U3>::from_bits(11 << 3));
[598](#598)assert_eq!(eleven, 11);
[599](#599)assert_eq!(eleven.to_string(), \"11\");
[600](#600)let two_point_75 = eleven / 4;
[601](#601)assert_eq!(two_point_75, ", stringify!($Self), "::<U3>::from_bits(11 << 1));
[602](#602)assert_eq!(two_point_75, 2.75);
[603](#603)assert_eq!(two_point_75.to_string(), \"2.8\");
[604](#604)```
[605](#605)
[606](#606)[*typenum* crate]: https://crates.io/crates/typenum
[607](#607)[U", $n, "]: crate::types::extra::U", $n, "
[608](#608)[U0]: crate::types::extra::U0
[609](#609)";
[610](#610)            #[repr(transparent)]
[611](#611)            pub struct $Self<Frac> {
[612](#612)                pub(crate) bits: $Inner,
[613](#613)                phantom: PhantomData<Frac>,
[614](#614)            }
[615](#615)        }
[616](#616)
[617](#617)        impl<Frac> Clone for $Self<Frac> {
[618](#618)            #[inline]
[619](#619)            fn clone(&self) -> $Self<Frac> {
[620](#620)                *self
[621](#621)            }
[622](#622)        }
[623](#623)
[624](#624)        impl<Frac> Copy for $Self<Frac> {}
[625](#625)
[626](#626)        impl<Frac> Default for $Self<Frac> {
[627](#627)            #[inline]
[628](#628)            fn default() -> Self {
[629](#629)                $Self {
[630](#630)                    bits: Default::default(),
[631](#631)                    phantom: PhantomData,
[632](#632)                }
[633](#633)            }
[634](#634)        }
[635](#635)
[636](#636)        impl<Frac> Hash for $Self<Frac> {
[637](#637)            #[inline]
[638](#638)            fn hash<H: Hasher>(&self, state: &mut H) {
[639](#639)                self.bits.hash(state);
[640](#640)            }
[641](#641)        }
[642](#642)
[643](#643)        fixed_no_frac! {
[645](#645)            {Self, Inner} = {$Self, $Inner},
[646](#646)            Signedness = $Signedness,
[647](#647)            LeEqU = $LeEqU,
[648](#648)            {Unm1, Un} = {$Unm1, $Un},
[649](#649)            [nm4 ..= np1] = [$nm4, $nm3, $nm2, $nm1, $n, $np1],
[650](#650)            {ISelf, IInner} = {$ISelf, $IInner},
[651](#651)            {USelf, UInner} = {$USelf, $UInner},
[652](#652)            nbytes = $nbytes,
[653](#653)            {bytes_val, rev_bytes_val} = {$bytes_val, $rev_bytes_val},
[654](#654)            {be_bytes, le_bytes} = {$be_bytes, $le_bytes},
[655](#655)            $(
[656](#656)                n2 = $n2,
[657](#657)                {Double, DoubleInner} = {$Double, $DoubleInner},
[658](#658)                {IDouble, IDoubleInner} = {$IDouble, $IDoubleInner},
[659](#659)            )?
[660](#660)        }
[661](#661)        fixed_frac! {
[663](#663)            {Self, Inner} = {$Self, $Inner},
[664](#664)            Signedness = $Signedness,
[665](#665)            LeEqU = $LeEqU,
[666](#666)            {nm4, nm1, n} = {$nm4, $nm1, $n},
[667](#667)            {USelf, UInner} = {$USelf, $UInner},
[668](#668)        }
[669](#669)        fixed_const! {
[670](#670)            Self = $Self,
[671](#671)            Signedness = $Signedness,
[672](#672)            LeEqU = $LeEqU,
[673](#673)            [nm4 ..= n] = [$nm4, $nm3, $nm2, $nm1, $n],
[674](#674)            [LeEqUC0 ..= LeEqUC3] = [$LeEqUC0, $LeEqUC1, $LeEqUC2, $LeEqUC3],
[675](#675)        }
[676](#676)    };

# FixedI8 in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/struct.FixedI8.html

`pub struct FixedI8<Frac> { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An eight-bit signed number with `Frac` fractional bits.

The number has 8 bits, of which *f* = `Frac` are
fractional bits and 8 − *f* are integer bits.
The value *x* can lie in the range −27/2 f ≤

*x*< 2

7/2

. The difference between successive numbers is constant throughout the range:

*f**Δ*= 1/2

.

*f*For `FixedI8<`, [U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*f* = 0 and
*Δ* = 1, and the fixed-point number behaves like an [ i8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i8.html) with the value lying in the range −2

7≤

*x*< 2

7. For

`FixedI8<`[U8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U8.html)>,
*f*= 8 and

*Δ*= 1/2

8, and the value lies in the range −1/2 ≤

*x*< 1/2.

`Frac` is an [ Unsigned](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.Unsigned.html) as provided by the

[.](https://crates.io/crates/typenum)

*typenum*crate`FixedI8<Frac>` has the same size, alignment and ABI as
[ i8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i8.html); it is

`#[repr(transparent)]` with
[as the only non-zero-sized field.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i8.html)

`i8`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U3;
use fixed::FixedI8;
let eleven = FixedI8::<U3>::from_num(11);
assert_eq!(eleven, FixedI8::<U3>::from_bits(11 << 3));
assert_eq!(eleven, 11);
assert_eq!(eleven.to_string(), "11");
let two_point_75 = eleven / 4;
assert_eq!(two_point_75, FixedI8::<U3>::from_bits(11 << 1));
assert_eq!(two_point_75, 2.75);
assert_eq!(two_point_75.to_string(), "2.8");
```

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-FixedI8%3CFrac%3E)

### impl<Frac> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

The implementation of items in this block is independent
of the number of fractional bits `Frac`.

The difference between any two successive representable numbers, *Δ*.

If the number has *f* = `Frac` fractional bits, then
*Δ* = 1/2 f.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::DELTA, Fix::from_bits(1));
// binary 0.0001 is decimal 0.0625
assert_eq!(Fix::DELTA, 0.0625);
```
The smallest value that can be represented.

If the number has *f* = `Frac` fractional bits,
then the minimum is −27/2 f.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::MIN, Fix::from_bits(i8::MIN));
```
The largest value that can be represented.

If the number has *f* = `Frac` fractional bits, then the maximum is
(27 − 1)/2 f.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-4)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX, Fix::from_bits(i8::MAX));
```
Creates a fixed-point number that has a bitwise representation identical to the given integer.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 0010.0000 = 2
assert_eq!(Fix::from_bits(0b10_0000), 2);
```
Creates an integer that has a bitwise representation identical to the given fixed-point number.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 2 is 0010.0000
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(2).to_bits(), 0b10_0000);
```
Converts a fixed-point number from big endian to the target’s endianness.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
let f = Fix::from_bits(0x12);
if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(Fix::from_be(f), f);
} else {
    assert_eq!(Fix::from_be(f), f.swap_bytes());
}
```
Converts a fixed-point number from little endian to the target’s endianness.

Multiplies two fixed-point numbers and returns a wider type to retain all precision.

If `self` has *f* fractional bits and 8 − *f*
integer bits, and `rhs` has *g* fractional bits and 8 − *g* integer bits, then the returned fixed-point number will
have *f* + *g* fractional bits and 16 − *f* − *g* integer bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-33)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U2, U4};
use fixed::FixedI8;
// decimal: 1.25 × 1.0625 = 1.328_125
// binary: 1.01 × 1.0001 = 1.010101
let a = FixedI8::<U2>::from_num(1.25);
let b = FixedI8::<U4>::from_num(1.0625);
assert_eq!(a.wide_mul(b), 1.328_125);
```

Divides two fixed-point numbers and returns a wider type to retain more precision.

If `self` has *f* fractional bits
and 8 − *f* integer bits, and `rhs` has
*g* fractional bits and 8 − *g* integer
bits, then the returned fixed-point number will
have 8 + *f* − *g* fractional
bits and 8 − *f* + *g* integer
bits.

**Warning:** While most cases of overflow are avoided using this method,
dividing [ MIN](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.MIN) by

`-`[DELTA](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA) will still
result in panic due to overflow. The alternative [method avoids this by sacrificing one fractional bit in the return type.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wide_sdiv)

`wide_sdiv`[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the divisor is zero or on overflow. Overflow can only occur when dividing
[ MIN](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.MIN) by

`-`[DELTA](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA).[§](https://docs.rs#examples-35)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U3, U5, U6};
use fixed::{FixedI8, FixedI16};
// decimal: 4.625 / 0.03125 = 148
// binary: 100.101 / 0.00001 = 10010100
let a = FixedI8::<U3>::from_num(4.625);
let b = FixedI8::<U5>::from_num(0.03125);
let ans: FixedI16<U6> = a.wide_div(b);
assert_eq!(ans, 148);
```
The following panics because of overflow.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

Divides two fixed-point numbers and returns a wider type to retain more precision.

If `self` has *f* fractional bits and
8 − *f*
integer bits, and `rhs` has *g* fractional bits and
8 − *g*
integer bits, then the returned fixed-point number will have
7 + *f* − *g*
fractional bits and
9 − *f* + *g*
integer bits.

This is similar to the [ wide_div](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wide_div) method but
sacrifices one fractional bit to avoid overflow.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

Panics if the divisor is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-36)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U4, U5, U6};
use fixed::{FixedI8, FixedI16};
// decimal: 4.625 / 0.03125 = 148
// binary: 100.101 / 0.00001 = 10010100
let a = FixedI8::<U4>::from_num(4.625);
let b = FixedI8::<U5>::from_num(0.03125);
let ans: FixedI16<U6> = a.wide_sdiv(b);
assert_eq!(ans, 148);
```
Unlike [ wide_div](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wide_div), dividing

[by](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN``-`[DELTA](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA) does not overflow.```
use fixed::types::extra::{U4, U7};
use fixed::{FixedI8, FixedI16};
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
type DFix = FixedI16<U7>;
assert_eq!(Fix::MIN.wide_sdiv(-Fix::DELTA), (DFix::MIN / 2).abs());
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

Multiply and add. Returns `self` × `mul` + `add`.

For some cases, the product `self` × `mul` would overflow
on its own, but the final result `self` × `mul` + `add` is representable; in
these cases this method returns the correct result without overflow.

The `mul` parameter can have a fixed-point type like
`self` but with a different number of fractional bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

When debug assertions are enabled, this method panics if the result
overflows. When debug assertions are not enabled, the wrapped value
can be returned, but it is not considered a breaking change if in the
future it panics; if wrapping is required use [ wrapping_mul_add](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wrapping_mul_add)
instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-38)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(4).mul_add(Fix::from_num(0.5), Fix::from_num(3)),
    Fix::from_num(5)
);
// MAX × 1.5 - MAX = MAX / 2, which does not overflow
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.mul_add(Fix::from_num(1.5), -Fix::MAX), Fix::MAX / 2);
```

Returns the mean of `self` and `other`.

This method rounds the result down towards −∞. This is different from the
standard library [ midpoint](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i8.html#method.midpoint), which rounds
towards 0. Rounding down preserves translation invariance, that is

`(a + t).mean(b + t)` = `a.mean(b) + t`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-46)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(3).mean(Fix::from_num(4)), Fix::from_num(3.5));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(-3).mean(Fix::from_num(4)), Fix::from_num(0.5));
```
Compute the hypotenuse of a right triange.

The hypotenuse is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of the operands.

This method uses an iterative method for its square root, with up to 8
iterations for [ FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html). The result is rounded down, and the
error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

Checked multiply and add.
Returns `self` × `mul` + `add`, or [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) on overflow.

For some cases, the product `self` × `mul` would overflow
on its own, but the final result `self` × `mul` + `add` is representable; in
these cases this method returns the correct result without overflow.

The `mul` parameter can have a fixed-point type like
`self` but with a different number of fractional bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-60)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(4).checked_mul_add(Fix::from_num(0.5), Fix::from_num(3)),
    Some(Fix::from_num(5))
);
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.checked_mul_add(Fix::ONE, Fix::ZERO), Some(Fix::MAX));
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.checked_mul_add(Fix::ONE, Fix::DELTA), None);
// MAX × 1.5 - MAX = MAX / 2, which does not overflow
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.checked_mul_add(Fix::from_num(1.5), -Fix::MAX), Some(Fix::MAX / 2));
```

Compute the hypotenuse of a right triange, returning [ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) on overflow.

The hypotenuse is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of the operands.

This method uses an iterative method for its square root, with up to 8
iterations for [ FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html). The result is rounded down, and the
error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA``self`² + `other`²) < result + `DELTA`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-68)Examples

```

use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// hypot(3, 4) == 5
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(3).checked_hypot(Fix::from_num(4)),
    Some(Fix::from_num(5))
);
// hypot(2, 7.875) == 8.125, which does not fit
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(2).checked_hypot(Fix::from_num(7.875)),
    None
);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)#### pub const fn [saturating_mul_add](https://docs.rs#method.saturating_mul_add)<MulFrac: [LeEqU8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.LeEqU8.html)>(
    self,
    mul: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<MulFrac>,
    add: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

#### pub const fn [saturating_mul_add](https://docs.rs#method.saturating_mul_add)<MulFrac: [LeEqU8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.LeEqU8.html)>(
    self,
    mul: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<MulFrac>,
    add: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

Saturating multiply and add.
Returns `self` × `mul` + `add`, saturating on overflow.

For some cases, the product `self` × `mul` would overflow
on its own, but the final result `self` × `mul` + `add` is representable; in
these cases this method returns the correct result without overflow.

The `mul` parameter can have a fixed-point type like
`self` but with a different number of fractional bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-76)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(4).saturating_mul_add(Fix::from_num(0.5), Fix::from_num(3)),
    Fix::from_num(5)
);
let half_max = Fix::MAX / 2;
assert_eq!(half_max.saturating_mul_add(Fix::from_num(3), half_max), Fix::MAX);
assert_eq!(half_max.saturating_mul_add(Fix::from_num(-5), half_max), Fix::MIN);
// MAX × 1.5 - MAX = MAX / 2, which does not overflow
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.saturating_mul_add(Fix::from_num(1.5), -Fix::MAX), half_max);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)#### pub const fn [saturating_hypot](https://docs.rs#method.saturating_hypot)(self, other: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

#### pub const fn [saturating_hypot](https://docs.rs#method.saturating_hypot)(self, other: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

Compute the hypotenuse of a right triange, saturating on overflow.

The hypotenuse is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of the operands.

This method uses an iterative method for its square root, with up to 8
iterations for [ FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html). The result is rounded down, and the
error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA``self`² + `other`²) < result + `DELTA`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-81)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// hypot(3, 4) == 5
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(3).saturating_hypot(Fix::from_num(4)),
    Fix::from_num(5)
);
// hypot(2, 7.875) == 8.125, which does not fit
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(2).saturating_hypot(Fix::from_num(7.875)),
    Fix::MAX
);
```

Inverse linear interpolation between `start` and `end`,
saturating on overflow.

The computed value can have a fixed-point type like `self` but with a different
number of fractional bits.

Returns
(`self` − `start`) / (`end` − `start`).
This is 0 when `self` = `start`, and 1 when `self` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-13)Panics

Panics when `start` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-83)Examples

```

use fixed::FixedI8;

let four = Fix::from_num(4);
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(3).saturating_inv_lerp::<U4>(two, four), 0.5);
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.saturating_inv_lerp::<U4>(Fix::ZERO, Fix::from_num(0.5)), Fix::MAX);
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.saturating_inv_lerp::<U4>(Fix::from_num(0.5), Fix::ZERO), Fix::MIN);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)#### pub const fn [wrapping_hypot](https://docs.rs#method.wrapping_hypot)(self, other: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

#### pub const fn [wrapping_hypot](https://docs.rs#method.wrapping_hypot)(self, other: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

Compute the hypotenuse of a right triange, wrapping on overflow.

The hypotenuse is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of the operands.

This method uses an iterative method for its square root, with up to 8
iterations for [ FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html). The result is rounded down, and the
error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA``self`² + `other`²) < result + `DELTA`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-96)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// hypot(3, 4) == 5
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(3).wrapping_hypot(Fix::from_num(4)),
    Fix::from_num(5)
);
// hypot(2, 7.875) == 8.125, which wraps to -7.875
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(2).wrapping_hypot(Fix::from_num(7.875)),
    Fix::from_num(-7.875)
);
```

    self,

#### pub const fn [wrapping_inv_lerp](https://docs.rs#method.wrapping_inv_lerp)<RetFrac: [LeEqU8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.LeEqU8.html)>(
    self,
    start: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
    end: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<RetFrac>

Inverse linear interpolation between `start` and `end`,
wrapping on overflow.

The computed value can have a fixed-point type like `self` but with a different
number of fractional bits.

Returns
(`self` − `start`) / (`end` − `start`).
This is 0 when `self` = `start`, and 1 when `self` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-16)Panics

Panics when `start` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-98)Examples

```

use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
let two = Fix::from_num(2);
let four = Fix::from_num(4);
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(3).wrapping_inv_lerp::<U4>(two, four), 0.5);
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.wrapping_inv_lerp::<U4>(Fix::ZERO, Fix::from_num(0.5)),
    Fix::MAX.wrapping_mul_int(2)
);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)#### pub const fn [strict_mul_add](https://docs.rs#method.strict_mul_add)<MulFrac: [LeEqU8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.LeEqU8.html)>(
    self,
    mul: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<MulFrac>,
    add: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

#### pub const fn [strict_mul_add](https://docs.rs#method.strict_mul_add)<MulFrac: [LeEqU8](https://docs.rs/types/extra/trait.LeEqU8.html)>(
    self,
    mul: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<MulFrac>,
    add: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>

Strict multiply and add.
Returns `self` × `mul` + `add`, panicking on overflow.

For some cases, the product `self` × `mul` would overflow
on its own, but the final result `self` × `mul` + `add` is representable; in
these cases this method returns the correct result without overflow.

The `mul` parameter can have a fixed-point type like
`self` but with a different number of fractional bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-21)Panics

Panics if the result does not fit.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-105)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(4).strict_mul_add(Fix::from_num(0.5), Fix::from_num(3)),
    Fix::from_num(5)
);
// MAX × 1.5 - MAX = MAX / 2, which does not overflow
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.strict_mul_add(Fix::from_num(1.5), -Fix::MAX), Fix::MAX / 2);
```
The following panics because of overflow.

This method uses an iterative method for its square root, with up to 8

error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA``self`² + `other`²) < result + `DELTA`.[§](https://docs.rs#panics-28)Panics

```

type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// hypot(3, 4) == 5

    Fix::from_num(3).overflowing_hypot(Fix::from_num(4)),
    (Fix::from_num(5), false)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

Overflowing multiply and add.

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of `self` × `mul` + `add` and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) indicating
whether an overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is
returned.

For some cases, the product `self` × `mul` would overflow
on its own, but the final result `self` × `mul` + `add` is representable; in
these cases this method returns the correct result without overflow.

The `mul` parameter can have a fixed-point type like
`self` but with a different number of fractional bits.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-121)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_mul_add(Fix::ONE, Fix::ZERO),
    (Fix::MAX, false)
);
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_mul_add(Fix::ONE, Fix::DELTA),
    (Fix::MIN, true)
);
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_mul_add(Fix::from_num(3), Fix::MAX),
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_mul_int(4)
);
// MAX × 1.5 - MAX = MAX / 2, which does not overflow
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_mul_add(Fix::from_num(1.5), -Fix::MAX),
    (Fix::MAX / 2, false)
);
```

Compute the hypotenuse of a right triange.

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of the hypotenuse and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html), indicating whether an
overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

The hypotenuse is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of the operands.

iterations for [ FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html). The result is rounded down, and the
error is <

[. That is, result ≤ √(](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA``self`² + `other`²) < result + `DELTA`.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-128)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// hypot(3, 4) == 5
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(3).overflowing_hypot(Fix::from_num(4)),
    (Fix::from_num(5), false)
);
// hypot(2, 7.875) == 8.125, which wraps to -7.875
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(2).overflowing_hypot(Fix::from_num(7.875)),
    (Fix::from_num(-7.875), true)
);
```

#### pub const fn [overflowing_next_multiple_of](https://docs.rs#method.overflowing_next_multiple_of)(
    self,
    other: [FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>,
) -> ([FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Overflowing next multiple of `other`.

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of the next multiple and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) indicating whether an
overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

The next multiple is the smallest multiple of `other` that is ≥ `self` if `other` is positive, and the largest multiple of
`other` that is ≤ `self` if `other` is negative.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-34)Panics

Panics if `other` is zero.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-129)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(4).overflowing_next_multiple_of(Fix::from_num(1.5)),
    (Fix::from_num(4.5), false)
);
let max_minus_delta = Fix::MAX - Fix::DELTA;
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_next_multiple_of(max_minus_delta),
    (max_minus_delta.wrapping_mul_int(2), true)
);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

Overflowing inverse linear interpolation between `start` and `end`.

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of the result and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) indicationg whether an overflow
has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

The computed value can have a fixed-point type like `self` but with a different
number of fractional bits.

Computes
(`self` − `start`) / (`end` − `start`).
This is 0 when `self` = `start`, and 1 when `self` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-35)Panics

Panics when `start` = `end`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-130)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
let two = Fix::from_num(2);
let four = Fix::from_num(4);
assert_eq!(
    Fix::from_num(3).overflowing_inv_lerp::<U4>(two, four),
    (Fix::from_num(0.5), false)
);
assert_eq!(
    Fix::MAX.overflowing_inv_lerp::<U4>(Fix::ZERO, Fix::from_num(0.5)),
    (Fix::MAX.wrapping_mul_int(2), true)
);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)[§](https://docs.rs#impl-FixedI8%3CFrac%3E-1)The implementation of items in this block depends on the
number of fractional bits `Frac`.

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

[§](https://docs.rs#impl-FixedI8%3CFrac%3E-1)

The implementation of items in this block depends on the
number of fractional bits `Frac`.

Creates a fixed-point number from another number.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other number `src`for which`ToFixed``src.`.[to_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html#tymethod.to_fixed)()

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-52)Panics

For floating-point numbers, panics if the value is not [finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html#method.is_finite).

When debug assertions are enabled, panics if the value does not fit.
When debug assertions are not enabled, the wrapped value can be
returned, but it is not considered a breaking change if in the future
it panics; if wrapping is required use [ wrapping_from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wrapping_from_num) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-135)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let src = I16F16::from_bits(0b111 << (16 - 2));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(src), Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(3i32), Fix::from_bits(3 << 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(-3i64), Fix::from_bits(-3 << 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(1.75f32), Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_num(-1.75f64), Fix::from_bits(-0b111 << (4-2)));
```
Converts a fixed-point number to another number.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other type `Dst`for which`FromFixed``Dst::`.[from_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html#tymethod.from_fixed)(self)

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-53)Panics

When debug assertions are enabled, panics if the value does not fit.
When debug assertions are not enabled, the wrapped value can be
returned, but it is not considered a breaking change if in the future
it panics; if wrapping is required use [ wrapping_to_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.wrapping_to_num) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-136)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::types::I30F2;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let src = Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2));
assert_eq!(src.to_num::<I30F2>(), I30F2::from_bits(0b111));
// src >> 2 is 0.0111, which for I30F2 is truncated to 0.01
assert_eq!((src >> 2u32).to_num::<I30F2>(), I30F2::from_bits(0b1));
// 2.5 is 10.1 in binary
let two_point_5 = Fix::from_bits(0b101 << (4 - 1));
assert_eq!(two_point_5.to_num::<i32>(), 2);
assert_eq!((-two_point_5).to_num::<i64>(), -3);
// 1.625 is 1.101 in binary
let one_point_625 = Fix::from_bits(0b1101 << (4 - 3));
assert_eq!(one_point_625.to_num::<f32>(), 1.625f32);
assert_eq!((-one_point_625).to_num::<f64>(), -1.625f64);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-55)Panics

For floating-point numbers, panics if the value is not [finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html#method.is_finite).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-141)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U0, U4};
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let src = I16F16::from_bits(0b111 << (16 - 2));
assert_eq!(Fix::wrapping_from_num(src), Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2)));
// integer 0b1101 << (8 - 7) will wrap to fixed-point 1010...
let too_large = FixedI8::<U0>::from_bits(0b1101 << (8 - 7));
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1010 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::wrapping_from_num(too_large), wrapped);
// integer 0b1101 << (8 - 7) will wrap to fixed-point 1010...
let large: i8 = 0b1101 << (8 - 7);
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1010 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::wrapping_from_num(large), wrapped);
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let expected = Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2));
assert_eq!(Fix::wrapping_from_num(1.75f32), expected);
// 1.75 << (8 - 4) wraps to binary 11000...
let large = 1.75 * 2f32.powi(8 - 4);
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1100 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::wrapping_from_num(large), wrapped);
```

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of the fixed-point number and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) indicating
whether an overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is
returned.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other number `src`for which`ToFixed``src.`.[overflowing_to_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html#tymethod.overflowing_to_fixed)()

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-58)Panics

For floating-point numbers, panics if the value is not [finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html#method.is_finite).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-145)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U0, U4};
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let src = I16F16::from_bits(0b111 << (16 - 2));
let expected = Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(src), (expected, false));
// integer 0b1101 << (8 - 7) will wrap to fixed-point 1010...
let too_large = FixedI8::<U0>::from_bits(0b1101 << (8 - 7));
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1010 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(too_large), (wrapped, true));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(3), (Fix::from_bits(3 << 4), false));
// integer 0b1101 << (8 - 7) will wrap to fixed-point 1010...
let large: i8 = 0b1101 << (8 - 7);
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1010 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(large), (wrapped, true));
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let expected = Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(1.75f32), (expected, false));
// 1.75 << (8 - 4) wraps to binary 11000...
let large = 1.75 * 2f32.powi(8 - 4);
let wrapped = Fix::from_bits(0b1100 << (8 - 4));
assert_eq!(Fix::overflowing_from_num(large), (wrapped, true));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)#### pub fn [overflowing_to_num](https://docs.rs#method.overflowing_to_num)<Dst: [FromFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html)>(self) -> (Dst, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/lib.rs.html#772-788)

#### pub fn [overflowing_to_num](https://docs.rs#method.overflowing_to_num)<Dst: [FromFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html)>(self) -> (Dst, [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html))

Converts a fixed-point number to another number.

Returns a [tuple](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.tuple.html) of the number and a [ bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) indicating whether an
overflow has occurred. On overflow, the wrapped value is returned.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other type `Dst`for which`FromFixed``Dst::`.[overflowing_from_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html#tymethod.overflowing_from_fixed)(self)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-146)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::{U0, U4, U6};
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.75 is 1.11 in binary
let src = Fix::from_bits(0b111 << (4 - 2));
let expected = I16F16::from_bits(0b111 << (16 - 2));
assert_eq!(src.overflowing_to_num::<I16F16>(), (expected, false));
type TooFewIntBits = FixedI8<U6>;
let wrapped = TooFewIntBits::from_bits(Fix::MAX.to_bits() << 2);
assert_eq!(Fix::MAX.overflowing_to_num::<TooFewIntBits>(), (wrapped, true));
// 2.5 is 10.1 in binary
let two_point_5 = Fix::from_bits(0b101 << (4 - 1));
assert_eq!(two_point_5.overflowing_to_num::<i32>(), (2, false));
let does_not_fit = FixedI8::<U0>::from_bits(-1);
let wrapped = 1u8.wrapping_neg();
assert_eq!(does_not_fit.overflowing_to_num::<u8>(), (wrapped, true));
// 1.625 is 1.101 in binary
let one_point_625 = Fix::from_bits(0b1101 << (4 - 3));
assert_eq!(one_point_625.overflowing_to_num::<f32>(), (1.625f32, false));
```

Parses a fixed-point literal.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

This is similar to [ from_str](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html#method.from_str) but accepts a prefix for setting
the radix, and ignores underscores, such that the parsing is more similar to
numeric literals in Rust code.

The string can start with “`-`” for a negative number.

Strings starting with “`0b`” are parsed as binary, strings
starting with “`0o`” are parsed as octal, and strings starting with “`0x`” are
parsed as hexadecimal.

Exponents are supported as well. For decimal, binary and octal numbers, the
separator “`e`” or “`E`” can be used to start an exponent, which is then
followed by an optional sign “`+`” or “`-`”, and then by a decimal integer which
is the exponent. For hexadecimal numbers, since “`e`” and “`E`” are hexadecimal
digits, the separator “`@`” has to be used instead. The separator “`@`” is
accepted for all radices. The parsed value is scaled by the radix to the power
of the exponent.

For binary, octal and hexadecimal, base-2 exponents are supported too, using the
separator “`p`” or “`P`”. The parsed value is scaled by 2 to the power of the
exponent. For example, for hexadecimal “`P8`” means ×2⁸, and is equivalent to
“`@2`” which means ×16².

[§](https://docs.rs#constants)Constants

The `lit` method is useful to write constant fixed-point literals, and can be
evaluated in constant context.

**Warning:** Normal calls to the `lit` method are *not* evaluated at compile
time. To ensure that the call is evaluated at compile time, `lit` must be used
in an inline constant expression, or used to initialize a constant.

For example, here `lit` would be evaluated at compile time:

`const ONE_AND_HALF: Fix = Fix::lit("1.5");`However, here `lit` would be evaluated at run time:

```
// Evaluated at run time.
let one_and_half = Fix::lit("1.5");
```
To evaluate at compile time without introducing a constant into the scope:

`let one_and_half = const { Fix::lit("1.5") };`[§](https://docs.rs#panics-61)Panics

Panics if the number is not valid or overflows.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-149)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("1.75"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("1_.7_5_"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("17.5e-1"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0_.017_5_e+0_2"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("-01.75"), -1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0b1.11"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0b_111e-2"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("-0b1.11"), -1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0o1.6"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0o.16E1"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0o7p-2"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0x1.C"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("0x0.1C@1"), 1.75);
assert_eq!(Fix::lit("-0x1.C"), -1.75);
```
This method is useful to write constant fixed-point literals.

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
const ONE_AND_HALF: Fix = Fix::lit("1.5");
assert_eq!(ONE_AND_HALF, 1.5);
```
Parses a string slice containing decimal digits to return a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

The number can have an optional exponent. The separator “`e`”, “`E`” or “`@`”
can be used to start an exponent, which is then followed by an optional sign
“`+`” or “`-`”, and then by a decimal integer which is the exponent. The parsed
value is scaled by 10 to the power of the exponent.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-150)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str("1.75"), Ok(Fix::from_num(1.75)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str("-1.75"), Ok(Fix::from_num(-1.75)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str("0.00625E+3"), Ok(Fix::from_num(6.25)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str("1.25e-1"), Ok(Fix::from_num(0.125)));
```

#### pub const fn [from_str_binary](https://docs.rs#method.from_str_binary)(
    src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html),

Parses a string slice containing binary digits to return a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

The number can have an optional exponent. The separator “`e`”, “`E`” or “`@`”
can be used to start an exponent, which is then followed by an optional sign
“`+`” or “`-`”, and then by a decimal integer which is the exponent. The parsed
value is scaled by the radix (2 for binary) to the power of the exponent.

Base-2 exponents are supported too, using the separator “`p`” or “`P`”. The
parsed value is scaled by 2 to the power of the exponent. For binary, since the
radix is 2, base-2 exponents are equivalent to the other form of exponent.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-151)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;
// 1.11 in binary is 1.75
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str_binary("1.11"), Ok(Fix::from_num(1.75)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str_binary("-1.11"), Ok(Fix::from_num(-1.75)));
// 111.0101 in binary is 7.3125
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str_binary("1.110101e2"), Ok(Fix::from_num(7.3125)));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str_binary("11101.01e-2"), Ok(Fix::from_num(7.3125)));
```

#### pub const fn [from_str_octal](https://docs.rs#method.from_str_octal)(src: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[FixedI8](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI8.html)<Frac>, [ParseFixedError](https://docs.rs/struct.ParseFixedError.html)>

Parses a string slice containing octal digits to return a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

The number can have an optional exponent. The separator “`e`”, “`E`” or “`@`”
can be used to start an exponent, which is then followed by an optional sign
“`+`” or “`-`”, and then by a decimal integer which is the exponent. The parsed
value is scaled by 8 to the power of the exponent.

Base-2 exponents are supported too, using the separator “`p`” or “`P`”. The
parsed value is scaled by 2 to the power of the exponent. For example, for octal
“`P6`” means ×2⁶, and is equivalent to “`E2`” which means ×8².

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-152)Examples

```
use fixed::types::extra::U4;
use fixed::FixedI8;
type Fix = FixedI8<U4>;

let neg = Fix::from_str_octal("-1.6");
assert_eq!(neg, Ok(-check));
assert_eq!(Fix::from_str_octal("160e-2"), Ok(check));
```

Parses a string slice containing hexadecimal digits to return a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

The number can have an optional exponent. Since “`e`” and “`E`” are valid
hexadecimal digits, they cannot be used as a separator to start an exponent, so

by 16 to the power of the exponent.

Base-2 exponents are supported too, using the separator “`p`” or “`P`”. The
parsed value is scaled by 2 to the power of the exponent. For example, for
hexadecimal “`P8`” means ×2⁸, and is equivalent to “`@2`” which means ×16².
