Returns the floating point category of the number.

If only one property is going to be tested, it is generally faster to use the specific predicate instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-6)Example

```
use core::num::FpCategory;
use fixed::F128;
assert_eq!(F128::ZERO.classify(), FpCategory::Zero);
assert_eq!(F128::MIN_POSITIVE_SUB.classify(), FpCategory::Subnormal);
assert_eq!(F128::MIN_POSITIVE.classify(), FpCategory::Normal);
assert_eq!(F128::INFINITY.classify(), FpCategory::Infinite);
assert_eq!(F128::NAN.classify(), FpCategory::Nan);
```
Returns the absolute value of the number.

The only difference possible between the input value and the returned value is in the sign bit, which is always cleared in the return value.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-7)Example

```
use fixed::F128;
// -0 == +0, but -0 bits != +0 bits
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_ZERO, F128::ZERO);
assert_ne!(F128::NEG_ZERO.to_bits(), F128::ZERO.to_bits());
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_ZERO.abs().to_bits(), F128::ZERO.to_bits());
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_INFINITY.abs(), F128::INFINITY);
assert_eq!(F128::MIN.abs(), F128::MAX);
assert!(F128::NAN.abs().is_nan());
```
Returns a number that represents the sign of the input value.

- 1 if the number is positive, +0, or +∞
- −1 if the number is negative, −0, or −∞
- NaN if the number is NaN

[§](https://docs.rs#example-8)Example

```
use fixed::F128;
assert_eq!(F128::ONE.signum(), F128::ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::INFINITY.signum(), F128::ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_ZERO.signum(), F128::NEG_ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::MIN.signum(), F128::NEG_ONE);
assert!(F128::NAN.signum().is_nan());
```
Returns a number composed of the magnitude of `self` and the sign of `sign`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-9)Example

```
use fixed::F128;
assert_eq!(F128::ONE.copysign(F128::NEG_ZERO), F128::NEG_ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::ONE.copysign(F128::ZERO), F128::ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_ONE.copysign(F128::NEG_INFINITY), F128::NEG_ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::NEG_ONE.copysign(F128::INFINITY), F128::ONE);
assert!(F128::NAN.copysign(F128::ONE).is_nan());
assert!(F128::NAN.copysign(F128::ONE).is_sign_positive());
assert!(F128::NAN.copysign(F128::NEG_ONE).is_sign_negative());
```

Clamps the value within the specified bounds.

Returns `min` if `self` < `min`, `max` if
`self` > `max`, or `self` otherwise.

Note that this method returns NaN if the initial value is NaN.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `min` > `max`, `min` is NaN, or `max` is NaN.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
use fixed::F128;
assert_eq!(F128::MIN.clamp(F128::NEG_ONE, F128::ONE), F128::NEG_ONE);
assert_eq!(F128::ZERO.clamp(F128::NEG_ONE, F128::ONE), F128::ZERO);
assert_eq!(F128::MAX.clamp(F128::NEG_ONE, F128::ONE), F128::ONE);
assert!(F128::NAN.clamp(F128::NEG_ONE, F128::ONE).is_nan());
```
Returns the ordering between `self` and `other`.

Unlike the [ PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) implementation, this method always returns an
order in the following sequence:

- NaN with the sign bit set
- −∞
- negative normal numbers
- negative subnormal numbers
- −0
- +0
- positive subnormal numbers
- positive normal numbers
- +∞
- NaN with the sign bit cleared

[§](https://docs.rs#example-14)Example

```
use core::cmp::Ordering;
use fixed::F128;
let neg_nan = F128::NAN.copysign(F128::NEG_ONE);
let pos_nan = F128::NAN.copysign(F128::ONE);
let neg_inf = F128::NEG_INFINITY;
let pos_inf = F128::INFINITY;
let neg_zero = F128::NEG_ZERO;
let pos_zero = F128::ZERO;
assert_eq!(neg_nan.total_cmp(&neg_inf), Ordering::Less);
assert_eq!(pos_nan.total_cmp(&pos_inf), Ordering::Greater);
assert_eq!(neg_zero.total_cmp(&pos_zero), Ordering::Less);
```

Converts a fixed-point number to a floating-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-1)Panics

When debug assertions are enabled, panics if the value
does not fit. When debug assertions are not enabled,
the wrapped value can be returned, but it is not
considered a breaking change if in the future it
panics; if wrapping is required use
[ wrapping_from_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html#tymethod.wrapping_from_fixed) instead.

### impl [PartialOrd](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/cmp/trait.PartialOrd.html) for [F128](https://docs.rs/struct.F128.html)

Converts a floating-point number to a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics-3)Panics

Panics if `self` is not [finite](https://docs.rs/struct.F128.html#method.is_finite).

When debug assertions are enabled, also panics if the value does not
fit. When debug assertions are not enabled, the wrapped value can be
returned, but it is not considered a breaking change if in the future
it panics; if wrapping is required use [ wrapping_to_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html#tymethod.wrapping_to_fixed) instead.

# fixed::prelude - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/prelude/index.html

## Expand description

A prelude to import useful traits.

This prelude is similar to the [standard library’s prelude](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/prelude/index.html) in
that you’ll almost always want to import its entire contents, but unlike the
standard library’s prelude you’ll have to do so manually:

`use fixed::prelude::*;`The prelude may grow over time as additional items see ubiquitous use.

[§](https://docs.rs#contents)Contents

The prelude re-exports the following:

- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)::{- [FromFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html),- [ToFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html)}
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)::{- [LossyFrom](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LossyFrom.html),- [LossyInto](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LossyInto.html)}
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)::{- [LosslessTryFrom](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LosslessTryFrom.html),- [LosslessTryInto](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LosslessTryInto.html)}

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use crate::traits::`- [FromFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html);
- `pub use crate::traits::`- [LosslessTryFrom](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LosslessTryFrom.html);
- `pub use crate::traits::`- [LosslessTryInto](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LosslessTryInto.html);
- `pub use crate::traits::`- [LossyFrom](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LossyFrom.html);
- `pub use crate::traits::`- [LossyInto](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.LossyInto.html);
- `pub use crate::traits::`- [ToFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html);

---

# fixed::traits - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/traits/index.html

## Expand description

Traits for conversions and for generic use of fixed-point numbers.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.Fixed.html)
- This trait provides methods common to all fixed-point numbers.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBits.html)- Bits
- This trait is implemented for [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.Fixed.html)::[Bits](https://docs.rs/trait.Fixed.html#associatedtype.Bits)
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBitsCast.html)- Bits - Cast
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `FixedBits`
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBitsOptionalArbitrary.html)- Bits - Optional - Arbitrary
- This trait is used to provide supertrait to the `FixedBits`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBitsOptionalBorsh.html)- Bits - Optional - Borsh
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `FixedBits`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBitsOptionalNum.html)- Bits - Optional - Num
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `FixedBits`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedBitsOptionalSerde.html)- Bits - Optional - Serde
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `FixedBits`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedEquiv.html)- Equiv
- This trait provides a way to convert a number to/from an equivalent fixed-point number.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalArbitrary.html)- Optional - Arbitrary
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalBorsh.html)- Optional - Borsh
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalFeatures.html)- Optional - Features
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalNightlyFloat.html)- Optional - Nightly - Float
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalNum.html)- Optional - Num
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedOptionalSerde.html)- Optional - Serde
- This trait is used to provide supertraits to the `Fixed`[optional features](https://docs.rs/index.html#optional-features), and should not be used directly.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedSigned.html)- Signed
- This trait provides methods common to all signed fixed-point numbers.
- [Fixed](https://docs.rs/trait.FixedUnsigned.html)- Unsigned
- This trait provides methods common to all unsigned fixed-point numbers.
- [From](https://docs.rs/trait.FromFixed.html)- Fixed
- This trait provides checked conversions from fixed-point numbers.
- [Lossless](https://docs.rs/trait.LosslessTryFrom.html)- TryFrom
- This trait provides lossless conversions that might be fallible.
- [Lossless](https://docs.rs/trait.LosslessTryInto.html)- TryInto
- This trait provides lossless conversions that might be fallible.
This is the reciprocal of `LosslessTryFrom`
- [Lossy](https://docs.rs/trait.LossyFrom.html)- From
- This trait provides infallible conversions that might be lossy.
- [Lossy](https://docs.rs/trait.LossyInto.html)- Into
- This trait provides infallible conversions that might be lossy.
This is the reciprocal of `LossyFrom`
- [ToFixed](https://docs.rs/trait.ToFixed.html)
- This trait provides checked conversions to fixed-point numbers.

# const_fixed_from_int in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/macro.const_fixed_from_int.html

```
macro_rules! const_fixed_from_int {
    ($($vis:vis const $NAME:ident: $Fixed:ty = $int:expr;)*) => { ... };
}
```
use the `const_from_int` method instead

## Expand description

Defines constant fixed-point numbers from integer expressions.

This macro was useful because [ from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num) cannot be
used in constant expressions. Now constant fixed-point numbers can be
created using the

[method or the](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.const_from_int)

`const_from_int`[method, so this macro is deprecated.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit)

`lit`[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fixed::const_fixed_from_int;
use fixed::types::I16F16;
const_fixed_from_int! {
    // define a constant using an integer
    const FIVE: I16F16 = 5;
    // define a constant using an integer expression
    const SUM: I16F16 = 3 + 2;
}
assert_eq!(FIVE, 5);
assert_eq!(SUM, 5);
```
This can now be rewritten as

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
const FIVE: I16F16 = I16F16::const_from_int(5);
const SUM: I16F16 = I16F16::const_from_int(3 + 2);
assert_eq!(FIVE, 5);
assert_eq!(SUM, 5);
```

# ParseFixedError in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/struct.ParseFixedError.html

`pub struct ParseFixedError { /* private fields */ }`## Expand description

An error which can be returned when parsing a fixed-point number.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::ParseFixedError;
// This string is not a fixed-point number.
let s = "something completely different (_!_!_)";
let error: ParseFixedError = match s.parse::<I16F16>() {
    Ok(_) => unreachable!(),
    Err(error) => error,
};
println!("Parse error: {error}");
```

# Saturating in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/struct.Saturating.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct Saturating<F>(pub F);`## Expand description

Provides saturating arithmetic on fixed-point numbers.

The underlying value can be retrieved through the `.0` index.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
let max = Saturating(I16F16::MAX);
let delta = Saturating(I16F16::DELTA);
assert_eq!(I16F16::MAX, (max + delta).0);
```

Converts a fixed-point number from big endian to the target’s endianness.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[from_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_be)`FixedU32::`.[from_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.from_be)

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
let w = Saturating(I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678));
if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(Saturating::from_be(w), w);
} else {
    assert_eq!(Saturating::from_be(w), w.swap_bytes());
}
```

Reverses the byte order of the fixed-point number.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[swap_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.swap_bytes)`FixedU32::`.[swap_bytes](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.swap_bytes)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-14)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
let w = Saturating(I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678));
let swapped = Saturating(I16F16::from_bits(0x7856_3412));
assert_eq!(w.swap_bytes(), swapped);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#490-492)#### pub fn [from_num](https://docs.rs#method.from_num)<Src: [ToFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html)>(src: Src) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#490-492)

#### pub fn [from_num](https://docs.rs#method.from_num)<Src: [ToFixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html)>(src: Src) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Saturating conversion from another number.

The other number can be:

- A fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type
[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other number `src`for which`ToFixed`[Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)(src.[saturating_to_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html#tymethod.saturating_to_fixed)())

See also
`FixedI32::`
and
[saturating_from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_from_num)`FixedU32::`.[saturating_from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.saturating_from_num)

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

For floating-point numbers, panics if the value is NaN.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I16F16};
use fixed::Saturating;
let src = I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678);
let dst = Saturating::<I4F4>::from_num(src);
assert_eq!(dst, Saturating(I4F4::MAX));
let src_int = 0x1234_i32;
let dst_int = Saturating::<I4F4>::from_num(src_int);
assert_eq!(dst_int, Saturating(I4F4::MAX));
let src_float = f64::NEG_INFINITY;
let dst_float = Saturating::<I4F4>::from_num(src_float);
assert_eq!(dst_float, Saturating(I4F4::MIN));
```
Converts a fixed-point number to another number, saturating the value on overflow.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type
[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other type `Dst`for which`FromFixed``Dst::`.[saturating_from_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html#tymethod.saturating_from_fixed)(self.0)

See also `FixedI32::` and
[saturating_to_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_to_num)`FixedU32::`.[saturating_to_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.saturating_to_num)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I16F16, I2F6, I4F4};
use fixed::Saturating;
// conversion that fits
let src = Saturating(I4F4::from_num(1.75));
let expected = I16F16::from_num(1.75);
assert_eq!(src.to_num::<I16F16>(), expected);
// conversion that saturates
let src = Saturating(I4F4::MAX);
assert_eq!(src.to_num::<I2F6>(), I2F6::MAX);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#717-719)#### pub fn [int](https://docs.rs#method.int)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#717-719)

#### pub fn [int](https://docs.rs#method.int)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Returns the integer part.

Note that since the numbers are stored in two’s complement,
negative numbers with non-zero fractional parts will be
rounded towards −∞, except in the case where there are no
integer bits, for example for the type
[Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>

See also `FixedI32::` and
[int](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.int)`FixedU32::`.[int](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.int)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-30)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
assert_eq!(Saturating(I16F16::from_num(12.25)).int(), Saturating(I16F16::from_num(12)));
assert_eq!(Saturating(I16F16::from_num(-12.25)).int(), Saturating(I16F16::from_num(-13)));
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#745-747)#### pub fn [frac](https://docs.rs#method.frac)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#745-747)

#### pub fn [frac](https://docs.rs#method.frac)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Returns the fractional part.

Note that since the numbers are stored in two’s complement,
the returned fraction will be non-negative for negative
numbers, except in the case where there are no integer bits,
for example for the type
[Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>`self`.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[frac](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.frac)`FixedU32::`.[frac](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.frac)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
assert_eq!(Saturating(I16F16::from_num(12.25)).frac(), Saturating(I16F16::from_num(0.25)));
assert_eq!(Saturating(I16F16::from_num(-12.25)).frac(), Saturating(I16F16::from_num(0.75)));
```

#### pub fn [round](https://docs.rs#method.round)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Saturating round. Rounds to the next integer to the nearest, with ties rounded away from zero, and saturating on overflow.

See also
`FixedI32::` and
[saturating_round](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_round)`FixedU32::`.[saturating_round](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.saturating_round)

assert_eq!((-two_half).round(), Saturating(I16F16::from_num(-3)));
let max = Saturating(I16F16::MAX);
assert_eq!(max.round(), max);
```

#### pub fn [signed_bits](https://docs.rs#method.signed_bits)(self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

Returns the number of bits required to represent the value.

The number of bits required includes an initial one for negative numbers, and an initial zero for non-negative numbers.

See also `FixedI32::`.[signed_bits](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.signed_bits)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-65)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I4F4;
use fixed::Saturating;
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(-3)).signed_bits(), 7);      // “_101.0000”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(-1)).signed_bits(), 5);      // “___1.0000”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(-0.0625)).signed_bits(), 1); // “____.___1”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(0)).signed_bits(), 1);       // “____.___0”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(0.0625)).signed_bits(), 2);  // “____.__01”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(1)).signed_bits(), 6);       // “__01.0000”
assert_eq!(Saturating(I4F4::from_num(3)).signed_bits(), 7);       // “_011.0000”
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#1684-1686)#### pub fn [signum](https://docs.rs#method.signum)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#1684-1686)

#### pub fn [signum](https://docs.rs#method.signum)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Returns a number representing the sign of `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

Using this method when 1 and −1 cannot be represented is almost certainly a bug, however, this is allowed and gives the following saturated results.

- When there are no integer bits, for example for the type
[Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>`self`is zero,`MIN``self`is negative, and`MAX``self`is positive.
- When there is one integer bit, for example for the type
[Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<[I1F15](https://docs.rs/types/type.I1F15.html)>`self`is zero, −1 when`self`is negative, and`MAX``self`is positive.

See also
`FixedI32::`.[saturating_signum](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_signum)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-69)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I0F32, I1F31, I16F16};
use fixed::Saturating;
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I16F16>::from_num(-3.9)).signum(), Saturating(I16F16::NEG_ONE));
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I16F16>::ZERO).signum(), Saturating(I16F16::ZERO));
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I16F16>::from_num(3.9)).signum(), Saturating(I16F16::ONE));
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I1F31>::from_num(0.5)).signum(), Saturating(I1F31::MAX));
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I0F32>::from_num(0.25)).signum(), Saturating(I0F32::MAX));
assert_eq!(Saturating(<I0F32>::from_num(-0.5)).signum(), Saturating(I0F32::MIN));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#1822-1824)#### pub fn [highest_one](https://docs.rs#method.highest_one)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/saturating.rs.html#1822-1824)

#### pub fn [highest_one](https://docs.rs#method.highest_one)(self) -> [Saturating](https://docs.rs/struct.Saturating.html)<F>

Returns the highest one in the binary representation, or zero
if `self` is zero.

If `self` > 0, the highest one is equal to the largest power
of two that is ≤ `self`.

See also `FixedU32::`.[highest_one](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.highest_one)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-75)Examples

```
use fixed::types::U16F16;
use fixed::Saturating;
type Sa = Saturating<U16F16>;
assert_eq!(Sa::from_bits(0b11_0010).highest_one(), Sa::from_bits(0b10_0000));
assert_eq!(Sa::from_num(0.3).highest_one(), Sa::from_num(0.25));
assert_eq!(Sa::from_num(4).highest_one(), Sa::from_num(4));
assert_eq!(Sa::from_num(6.5).highest_one(), Sa::from_num(4));
assert_eq!(Sa::ZERO.highest_one(), Sa::ZERO);
```

# Strict in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/struct.Strict.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct Strict<F>(pub F);`## Expand description

Provides arithmetic operations that panic on overflow even when debug assertions are disabled.

The underlying value can be retrieved through the `.0` index.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

This panics even when debug assertions are disabled.

## Tuple Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

negative numbers with non-zero fractional parts will be
rounded towards −∞, except in the case where there are no

```
Returns the fractional part.

Note that since the numbers are stored in two’s complement,
the returned fraction will be non-negative for negative
numbers, except in the case where there are no integer bits,
for example for the type
[Strict](https://docs.rs/struct.Strict.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>`self`.

## Trait Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#trait-implementations)

Parses a string slice containing decimal digits to return a fixed-point number.

Rounding is to the nearest, with ties rounded to even.

This method either returns [ Ok](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Ok) or panics, and never returns

[. The inherent method](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html#variant.Err)

`Err`[Strict](https://docs.rs/struct.Strict.html)<F>::[from_str_dec](https://docs.rs/struct.Strict.html#method.from_str_dec)[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)

`Result`[§](https://docs.rs#panics-37)Panics

Panics if the value does not fit or if there is a parsing error.

# Wrapping in fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/1.31.0/fixed/struct.Wrapping.html

`#[repr(transparent)]pub struct Wrapping<F>(pub F);`## Expand description

Provides intentionally wrapped arithmetic on fixed-point numbers.

The underlying value can be retrieved through the `.0` index.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
let max = Wrapping(I16F16::MAX);
let delta = Wrapping(I16F16::DELTA);
assert_eq!(I16F16::MIN, (max + delta).0);
```
## Tuple Fields[§](https://docs.rs#fields)

[§](https://docs.rs#structfield.0)

`0: F`## Implementations[§](https://docs.rs#implementations)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#149)#### pub const [FRAC_NBITS](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.FRAC_NBITS): [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) = F::FRAC_NBITS

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#149)

#### pub const [FRAC_NBITS](https://docs.rs#associatedconstant.FRAC_NBITS): [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html) = F::FRAC_NBITS

The number of fractional bits.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[FRAC_NBITS](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.FRAC_NBITS)`FixedU32::`.[FRAC_NBITS](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#associatedconstant.FRAC_NBITS)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(Wrapping::<I16F16>::FRAC_NBITS, I16F16::FRAC_NBITS);
```
Converts a fixed-point number from big endian to the target’s endianness.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[from_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_be)`FixedU32::`.[from_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.from_be)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
let w = Wrapping(I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678));
if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(Wrapping::from_be(w), w);
} else {
    assert_eq!(Wrapping::from_be(w), w.swap_bytes());
}
```
Converts a fixed-point number from little endian to the target’s endianness.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[from_le](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_le)`FixedU32::`.[from_le](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.from_le)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
let w = Wrapping(I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678));
if cfg!(target_endian = "little") {
    assert_eq!(Wrapping::from_le(w), w);
} else {
    assert_eq!(Wrapping::from_le(w), w.swap_bytes());
}
```
Converts `self` to big endian from the target’s endianness.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[to_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.to_be)`FixedU32::`.[to_be](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.to_be)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
let w = Wrapping(I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678));
if cfg!(target_endian = "big") {
    assert_eq!(w.to_be(), w);
} else {
    assert_eq!(w.to_be(), w.swap_bytes());
}
```
Converts `self` to little endian from the target’s endianness.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[to_le](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.to_le)`FixedU32::`.[to_le](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.to_le)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-13)Examples

```

    assert_eq!(w.to_le(), w);
} else {
    assert_eq!(w.to_le(), w.swap_bytes());
}
```

Wrapping conversion from another number.

The other number can be:

- A fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type
[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other number `src`for which`ToFixed`[Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)(src.[wrapping_to_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.ToFixed.html#tymethod.wrapping_to_fixed)())

See also
`FixedI32::`
and
[wrapping_from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_from_num)`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_from_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_from_num)

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

For floating-point numbers, panics if the value is not [finite](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html#method.is_finite).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-21)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I16F16};
use fixed::Wrapping;
// 0x1234.5678 wraps into 0x4.5
let src = I16F16::from_bits(0x1234_5678);
let dst = Wrapping::<I4F4>::from_num(src);
assert_eq!(dst, Wrapping(I4F4::from_bits(0x45)));
// 0x1234 wraps into 0x4.0
let src_int = 0x1234_i32;
let dst_int = Wrapping::<I4F4>::from_num(src_int);
assert_eq!(dst_int, Wrapping(I4F4::from_bits(0x40)));
// 129.75 wrapped into 1.75 (binary 1.1100)
let src_float = 129.75;
let dst_float = Wrapping::<I4F4>::from_num(src_float);
assert_eq!(dst_float, Wrapping(I4F4::from_bits(0b11100)));
```
Converts a fixed-point number to another number, wrapping the value on overflow.

The other number can be:

- Another fixed-point number. Any extra fractional bits are discarded, which rounds towards −∞.
- An integer of type `i8``i16``i32``i64``i128``isize``u8``u16``u32``u64``u128``usize`
- A floating-point number of type
[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)[half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/index.html)::[bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)`f32``f64``F128`
- Any other type `Dst`for which`FromFixed``Dst::`.[wrapping_from_fixed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.FromFixed.html#tymethod.wrapping_from_fixed)(self.0)

See also `FixedI32::` and
[wrapping_to_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_to_num)`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_to_num](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_to_num)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-22)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I16F16, I2F6, I4F4};
use fixed::Wrapping;
// conversion that fits
let src = Wrapping(I4F4::from_num(1.75));
let expected = I16F16::from_num(1.75);
assert_eq!(src.to_num::<I16F16>(), expected);
// conversion that wraps
let src = Wrapping(I4F4::MAX);
let wrapped = I2F6::from_bits(I2F6::MAX.to_bits() << 2);
assert_eq!(src.to_num::<I2F6>(), wrapped);
```

Returns the integer part.

Note that since the numbers are stored in two’s complement,
negative numbers with non-zero fractional parts will be
rounded towards −∞, except in the case where there are no
integer bits, for example for the type
[Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>

See also `FixedI32::` and
[int](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.int)`FixedU32::`.[int](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.int)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-30)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(12.25)).int(), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(12)));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(-12.25)).int(), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(-13)));
```
Returns the fractional part.

Note that since the numbers are stored in two’s complement,
the returned fraction will be non-negative for negative
numbers, except in the case where there are no integer bits,
for example for the type
[Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>`self`.

See also `FixedI32::` and
[frac](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.frac)`FixedU32::`.[frac](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.frac)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-31)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(12.25)).frac(), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(0.25)));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(-12.25)).frac(), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(0.75)));
```

```
Wrapping floor. Rounds to the next integer towards −∞, wrapping on overflow.

Overflow can only occur for signed numbers with zero integer bits.

See also
`FixedI32::` and
[wrapping_floor](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_floor)`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_floor](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_floor)

assert_eq!(Wrapping(I0F32::MIN).floor(), Wrapping(I0F32::ZERO));
```
Wrapping round. Rounds to the next integer to the nearest, with ties rounded away from zero, and wrapping on overflow.

See also
`FixedI32::` and
[wrapping_round](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_round)`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_round](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_round)

```

assert_eq!(num.div_euclid(den), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(3)));
let quarter = Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(0.25));
let check = (Wrapping(I16F16::MAX) * 4i32).round_to_zero();
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::MAX).div_euclid(quarter), check);
```

Wrapping absolute value. Returns the absolute value, wrapping on overflow.

Overflow can only occur when trying to find the absolute value of the minimum value.

See also `FixedI32::`.[wrapping_abs](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_abs)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-68)Examples

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(-5)).abs(), Wrapping(I16F16::from_num(5)));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(I16F16::MIN).abs(), Wrapping(I16F16::MIN));
```
Returns a number representing the sign of `self`.

[§](https://docs.rs#warning)Warning

Using this method when 1 and −1 cannot be represented is almost certainly a bug, however, this is allowed and gives the following wrapped results.

- When there are no integer bits, for example for the type
[Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<[I0F16](https://docs.rs/types/type.I0F16.html)>
- When there is one integer bit, for example for the type
[Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<[I1F15](https://docs.rs/types/type.I1F15.html)>`self`is zero, and −1 otherwise. This means that for a positive number, −1 is returned, because +1 does not fit and is wrapped to −1.

See also
`FixedI32::`.[wrapping_signum](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.wrapping_signum)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-69)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I0F32, I1F31, I16F16};
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I16F16>::from_num(-3.9)).signum(), Wrapping(I16F16::NEG_ONE));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I16F16>::ZERO).signum(), Wrapping(I16F16::ZERO));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I16F16>::from_num(3.9)).signum(), Wrapping(I16F16::ONE));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I1F31>::from_num(0.5)).signum(), Wrapping(I1F31::NEG_ONE));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I0F32>::from_num(0.25)).signum(), Wrapping(I0F32::ZERO));
assert_eq!(Wrapping(<I0F32>::from_num(-0.5)).signum(), Wrapping(I0F32::ZERO));
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#1825-1827)#### pub fn [highest_one](https://docs.rs#method.highest_one)(self) -> [Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#1825-1827)

#### pub fn [highest_one](https://docs.rs#method.highest_one)(self) -> [Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<F>

Returns the highest one in the binary representation, or zero
if `self` is zero.

If `self` > 0, the highest one is equal to the largest power
of two that is ≤ `self`.

See also `FixedU32::`.[highest_one](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.highest_one)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-75)Examples

```
use fixed::types::U16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
type T = Wrapping<U16F16>;
assert_eq!(T::from_bits(0b11_0010).highest_one(), T::from_bits(0b10_0000));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(0.3).highest_one(), T::from_num(0.25));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(4).highest_one(), T::from_num(4));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(6.5).highest_one(), T::from_num(4));
assert_eq!(T::ZERO.highest_one(), T::ZERO);
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#1851-1853)#### pub fn [next_power_of_two](https://docs.rs#method.next_power_of_two)(self) -> [Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<F>

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#1851-1853)

#### pub fn [next_power_of_two](https://docs.rs#method.next_power_of_two)(self) -> [Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<F>

Returns the smallest power of two that is ≥ `self`.

If the next power of two is too large to fit, it is wrapped to zero.

See also
`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_next_power_of_two](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_next_power_of_two)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-76)Examples

```
use fixed::types::U16F16;
use fixed::Wrapping;
type T = Wrapping<U16F16>;
assert_eq!(T::from_bits(0b11_0010).next_power_of_two(), T::from_bits(0b100_0000));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(0.3).next_power_of_two(), T::from_num(0.5));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(4).next_power_of_two(), T::from_num(4));
assert_eq!(T::from_num(6.5).next_power_of_two(), T::from_num(8));
// if the next power of two is too large, it is wrapped to zero
assert_eq!(T::MAX.next_power_of_two(), T::ZERO);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/fixed/wrapping.rs.html#1876-1878)

#### pub fn [add_signed](https://docs.rs#method.add_signed)(self, rhs: F::[Signed](https://docs.rs/traits/trait.Fixed.html#associatedtype.Signed)) -> [Wrapping](https://docs.rs/struct.Wrapping.html)<F>

Addition with an signed fixed-point number.

See also
`FixedU32::`.[wrapping_add_signed](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html#method.wrapping_add_signed)

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-77)Examples

```
use fixed::types::{I16F16, U16F16};
use fixed::Wrapping;
assert_eq!(
    Wrapping::<U16F16>::from_num(5).add_signed(I16F16::from_num(-3)),
    Wrapping::<U16F16>::from_num(2)
);
assert_eq!(
    Wrapping::<U16F16>::ZERO.add_signed(-I16F16::DELTA),
    Wrapping::<U16F16>::MAX
);
```

# fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/latest/aarch64-apple-darwin/fixed/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fixed-point-numbers)Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An *n*-bit fixed-point number has
*f* = `Frac`
fractional bits where
0 ≤ *f* ≤ *n*,
and
*n* − *f*
integer bits. For example, [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U24.html)>*n* = 32
total bits,
*f* = 24
fractional bits, and
*n* − *f* = 8
integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
*Δ* = 1/2 f.
When

*f*= 0, like in

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*Δ*= 1 because representable numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When

*f*=

*n*,

*Δ*= 1/2

and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤

*n**x*< 0.5 for signed numbers like

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>*x*< 1 for unsigned numbers like

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12::from_num(19) / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!(six_and_third.to_string(), "6.3333");
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil().to_num::<i32>(), 7);
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil(), 7);
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U12](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U12.html)>[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I4F12};
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4::from_num(1);
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!(ans1, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 3));
assert_eq!(ans1.to_string(), "3.2");
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12::from(a);
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4::from_num(wider_ans);
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!(ans2, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 6));
assert_eq!(ans2.to_string(), "3.4");
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`[§](https://docs.rs#comparing-fixed-point-numbers)Comparing fixed-point numbers

With floating-point numbers like [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), checking two numbers for equality can
require calculating both the absolute difference
(|

*a*−

*b*|) and the relative difference (|

*a*−

*b*| /

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements conversions and comparisons with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-optional-features)Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/aarch64-apple-darwin/half/index.html)::- [f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/aarch64-apple-darwin/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/aarch64-apple-darwin/half/index.html)::- [bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/aarch64-apple-darwin/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)

- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12::from_num(19) / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!(six_and_third.to_string(), "6.3333");
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil().to_num::<i32>(), 7);
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil(), 7);
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U12](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U12.html)>[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I4F12};
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4::from_num(1);
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!(ans1, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 3));
assert_eq!(ans1.to_string(), "3.2");
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12::from(a);
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4::from_num(wider_ans);
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!(ans2, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 6));
assert_eq!(ans2.to_string(), "3.4");
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`[§](https://docs.rs#comparing-fixed-point-numbers)Comparing fixed-point numbers

With floating-point numbers like [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), checking two numbers for equality can
require calculating both the absolute difference
(|

*a*−

*b*|) and the relative difference (|

*a*−

*b*| /

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```

# fixed - Rust

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fixed-point-numbers)Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An *n*-bit fixed-point number has
*f* = `Frac`
fractional bits where
0 ≤ *f* ≤ *n*,
and
*n* − *f*
integer bits. For example, [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U24.html)>*n* = 32
total bits,
*f* = 24
fractional bits, and
*n* − *f* = 8
integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
*Δ* = 1/2 f.
When

*f*= 0, like in

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*Δ*= 1 because representable numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When

*f*=

*n*,

*Δ*= 1/2

and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤

*n**x*< 0.5 for signed numbers like

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>*x*< 1 for unsigned numbers like

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

# fixed - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/fixed/latest/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/fixed/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#fixed-point-numbers)Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An *n*-bit fixed-point number has
*f* = `Frac`
fractional bits where
0 ≤ *f* ≤ *n*,
and
*n* − *f*
integer bits. For example, [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U24.html)>*n* = 32
total bits,
*f* = 24
fractional bits, and
*n* − *f* = 8
integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
*Δ* = 1/2 f.
When

*f*= 0, like in

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U0.html)>*Δ*= 1 because representable numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When

*f*=

*n*,

*Δ*= 1/2

and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤

*n**x*< 0.5 for signed numbers like

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>*x*< 1 for unsigned numbers like

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U32.html)>The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex``LowerExp``UpperExp`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-examples)Quick examples

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12::from_num(19) / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!(six_and_third.to_string(), "6.3333");
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil().to_num::<i32>(), 7);
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!(six_and_third.ceil(), 7);
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U12](https://docs.rs/types/extra/type.U12.html)>[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use fixed::types::{I4F4, I4F12};
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4::from_num(1);
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!(ans1, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 3));
assert_eq!(ans1.to_string(), "3.2");
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12::from(a);
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4::from_num(wider_ans);
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!(ans2, I4F4::from_bits((3 << 4) + 6));
assert_eq!(ans2.to_string(), "3.4");
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`[§](https://docs.rs#comparing-fixed-point-numbers)Comparing fixed-point numbers

With floating-point numbers like [ f32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f32.html), checking two numbers for equality can
require calculating both the absolute difference
(|

*a*−

*b*|) and the relative difference (|

*a*−

*b*| /

*a*) to account for rounding errors and different precisions.

With fixed-point numbers, this is simpler. Since the point is fixed, and very tiny numbers simply underflow to zero, it is usually enough to just check that the absolute difference between two numbers is smaller than a specific threshold.

You can do this using [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) and

[. For example to ensure that the difference between two numbers is less than 4 ×](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.DELTA)

`DELTA`*Δ*:

```
use fixed::types::I20F12;
let a = I20F12::from_num(1.5);
// b is not exactly 1.5 because of rounding errors
let b = a.sqrt() * a.sqrt();
// check for equality by comparing to 4 × Δ
assert!(a.saturating_dist(b) < 4 * I20F12::DELTA);
```
Note that [ saturating_dist](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.saturating_dist) was used instead of

[to avoid overflow if](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.dist)

`dist`*a*and

*b*are very different, for example

[and](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MIN)

`MIN`[.](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#associatedconstant.MAX)

`MAX`[§](https://docs.rs#writing-fixed-point-constants-and-values-literally)Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use fixed::types::I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0.127_5e2");
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16::lit("0x_18@-1");
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!(sum, 14.25);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#using-the-fixed-crate)Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies]
fixed = "1.31"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.93.0 or later.

[§](https://docs.rs#optional-features)Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate
- `compat-readonly-static`, disabled by default. This enables compatibility with platforms where statics are read-only by disabling caching of formatting flags in atomic statics. Note that this may incur a small performance overhead when formatting many numbers using the hexadecimal debug specifiers- `{:x?}`or- `{:X?}`.
- `defmt`, disabled by default. This implements formatting using the [- *defmt*crate]. Note that the implementation delegates to the- `Display`- `value.to_bits()`, and then decode on the host.
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently this is only required for the- `serde-str`feature.
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[dependencies.fixed]
features = ["serde"]
version = "1.31"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#experimental-optional-features)Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate
- `nightly-float`, disabled by default. This requires the nightly compiler, and implements conversions and comparisons with the experimental- `f16`- `f128`

[§](https://docs.rs#deprecated-optional-features)Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/half/index.html)::- [f16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/half/binary16/struct.f16.html)- [half](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/half/index.html)::- [bf16](https://docs.rs/half/2.7.1/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/half/bfloat/struct.bf16.html)
