## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ lit](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.22/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.lit) method, which is available as a

`const` function, can be used to
parse literals. It supports- underscores as separators;
- prefixes “`0b`”, “`0o`” and “`0x`” for binary, octal and hexadecimal numbers;
- an optional decimal exponent with separator “`e`” or “`E`” for decimal, binary and octal numbers, or with separator “`@`” for all supported radices including hexadecimal.

```
use I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16lit;
// 1.8 hexadecimal is 1.5 decimal, and 18@-1 is 1.8
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16lit;
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!;
```
The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) is an alternative which provides a convenient macro to
write down fixed-point constants literally in the code. It supports underscores
as separators, binary/octal/hexadecimal integers, and an optional exponent for
decimal numbers, but it does not support fractions or exponents for
binary/octal/hexadecimal as they cannot be parsed by the Rust compiler.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
use I16F16;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = fixed!;
// 11 binary is 3 decimal
const THREE: I16F16 = I16F16!;
// 12.75 + 3 = 15.75
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + THREE;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.22"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.61.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.22"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with const generics when the Rust
compiler’s [is ready and stabilized. An](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76560)

`generic_const_exprs` feature[alpha version](https://docs.rs/fixed/2.0.0-alpha/fixed/)is already available.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.20/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The parsing methods are available as `const` functions.

```
use I16F16;
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16unwrapped_from_str;
// 1.1 binary is 1.5 decimal
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16unwrapped_from_str_binary;
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!;
```
The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) is an alternative which provides a convenient macro to
write down fixed-point constants literally in the code. It supports underscores
as separators, scientific notation, and binary/octal/hexadecimal integers, but
it does not support binary/octal/hexadecimal fractions as they cannot be parsed
by the Rust compiler.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
// 11 binary is 3 decimal
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
// 12.75 + 3 = 15.75
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.20"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.61.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.20"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional
bits where 0 ≤ f ≤ n, and
n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits.
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like
in [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable
numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1.
When f = n, Δ = 1/2n
and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5
for signed numbers like [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.19/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with const generics when the Rust
compiler’s [is ready and stabilized. An](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76560)

`generic_const_exprs` feature[alpha version](https://docs.rs/fixed/2.0.0-alpha/fixed/)is already available.

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.18/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The parsing methods are available as `const` functions.

```
use I16F16;
const TWELVE_POINT_75: I16F16 = I16F16unwrapped_from_str;
// 1.1 binary is 1.5 decimal
const ONE_POINT_5: I16F16 = I16F16unwrapped_from_str_binary;
// 12.75 + 1.5 = 14.25
let sum = TWELVE_POINT_75 + ONE_POINT_5;
assert_eq!;
```
The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) is an alternative which provides a convenient macro to
write down fixed-point constants literally in the code. It supports underscores
as separators, scientific notation, and binary/octal/hexadecimal integers, but
it does not support binary/octal/hexadecimal fractions as they cannot be parsed
by the Rust compiler.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
// 0.1275e2 is 12.75
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
// 11 binary is 3 decimal
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
// 12.75 + 3 = 15.75
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.18"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.61.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.18"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

# fixed 1.17.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fixed/1.17.0

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional
bits where 0 ≤ f ≤ n, and
n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits.
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like
in [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable
numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1.
When f = n, Δ = 1/2n
and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5
for signed numbers like [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with const generics when the Rust
compiler’s [is ready and stabilized. An](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76560)

`generic_const_exprs` feature[alpha version](https://crates.io/crates/fixed/2.0.0-alpha.2)is already available.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.17/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional
bits where 0 ≤ f ≤ n, and
n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits.
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like
in [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable
numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1.
When f = n, Δ = 1/2n
and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5
for signed numbers like [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with const generics when the Rust
compiler’s [is ready and stabilized. An](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76560)

`generic_const_exprs` feature[alpha version](https://crates.io/crates/fixed/2.0.0-alpha.2)is already available.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.16/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) provides a convenient macro to write down fixed-point
constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.16"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.61.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.16"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like
in [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable
numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1.
When f = n, Δ = 1/2n
and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5
for signed numbers like [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with const generics when the Rust
compiler’s [is ready and stabilized. An](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/76560)

`generic_const_expr` feature[alpha version](https://crates.io/crates/fixed/2.0.0-alpha.2)is already available.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.15/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) provides a convenient macro to write down fixed-point
constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.15"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.57.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.15"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and will be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// -8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// -8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) provides a convenient macro to write down fixed-point
constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.13"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.57.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.13"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and may be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required for the- `az`
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required for conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`

# fixed 1.13.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fixed/1.13.0

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional
bits where 0 ≤ f ≤ n, and
n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits.
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like
in [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable
numbers are integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1.
When f = n, Δ = 1/2n
and the value lies in the range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5
for signed numbers like [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers like
[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with [const generics](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44580)instead when the Rust compiler support for them is powerful enough.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.13/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use it in your
crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.12"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.57.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `arbitrary`, disabled by default. This provides the generation of arbitrary fixed-point numbers from raw, unstructured data. This feature requires the- *arbitrary*crate
- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.12"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `borsh`, disabled by default. This implements serialization and deserialization using the- *borsh*crate- *borsh*crate
- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

# fixed 1.11.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/fixed/1.11.0

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional bits where
0 ≤ f ≤ n, and n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves
like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like in
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable numbers are
integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When
f = n, Δ = 1/2n and the value lies in the
range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5 for signed numbers like
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range 0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned
numbers like [FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with [const generics](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44580)instead when the Rust compiler support for them is powerful enough.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

- The `LeEqU8``LeEqU16``LeEqU32``LeEqU64``LeEqU128``'static`constraint, as it is a constraint of their supertrait`Unsigned`[version 1.14](https://docs.rs/typenum/~1.14/typenum/index.html). This fixes a potential compatibility issue introduced in version 1.9.0.
- An experimental feature was added to enable serialization using the *borsh*crate[merge request 9](https://gitlab.com/tspiteri/fixed/-/merge_requests/9)).

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// −8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// −8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.11/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

n − f = 8 integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves
like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like in
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable numbers are
integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When
f = n, Δ = 1/2n and the value lies in the
range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5 for signed numbers like
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range 0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned
numbers like [FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with [const generics](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44580)instead when the Rust compiler support for them is powerful enough.

The main features are

- Representation of binary fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide decimal fixed-point numbers. For example 0.001
cannot be represented exactly, as it is 1/103. It is binary fractions
like 1/24 (0.0625) that can be represented exactly, provided there
are enough fractional bits.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives are
provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Additionally, `az`
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`
- All fixed-point numbers are plain old data, so `bytemuck`

## Quick examples

```
use I20F12;
// 19/3 = 6 1/3
let six_and_third = I20F12from_num / 3;
// four decimal digits for 12 binary digits
assert_eq!;
// find the ceil and convert to i32
assert_eq!;
// we can also compare directly to integers
assert_eq!;
```
The type [ I20F12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.I20F12.html) is a 32-bit fixed-point signed number with 20 integer bits
and 12 fractional bits. It is an alias to

[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<

[U12](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/extra/type.U12.html)>. The unsigned counterpart would be

[. Aliases are provided for all combinations of integer and fractional bits adding up to a total of eight, 16, 32, 64 or 128 bits.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.U20F12.html)

`U20F12````
use ;
// −8 ≤ I4F4 < 8 with steps of 1/16 (~0.06)
let a = I4F4from_num;
// multiplication and division by integers are possible
let ans1 = a / 5 * 17;
// 1 / 5 × 17 = 3 2/5 (3.4), but we get 3 3/16 (~3.2)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// −8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low precision
of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to an inaccurate
result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision, we get `wider_a / 5`
equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate intermediate result `wider_ans` =
3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3
6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.9/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) provides a convenient macro to write down fixed-point
constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.9"
 = ["serde"]
```

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

An n-bit fixed-point number has f = `Frac` fractional bits where
0 ≤ f ≤ n, and n − f integer bits. For example,
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U24](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U24.html)> is a 32-bit signed fixed-point number with
n = 32 total bits, f = 24 fractional bits, and
n − f = 8 integer bits. [FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves
like [ i32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.i32.html), and

[FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<

[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)> behaves like

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)

`u32`The difference between any two successive representable numbers is constant
throughout the possible range for a fixed-point number:
Δ = 1/2f. When f = 0, like in
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U0](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U0.html)>, Δ = 1 because representable numbers are
integers, and the difference between two successive integers is 1. When
f = n, Δ = 1/2n and the value lies in the
range −0.5 ≤ x < 0.5 for signed numbers like
[FixedI32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>, and in the range 0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned
numbers like [FixedU32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/struct.FixedU32.html)<[U32](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.8/fixed/types/extra/type.U32.html)>.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit count

`Frac`;
the plan is to to have a major version 2 with [const generics](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44580)instead when the Rust compiler support for them is powerful enough.

The main features are

- Representation of fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no `log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate
- The *cordic*crate[CORDIC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CORDIC)algorithm.

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric

- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using `FromStr``from_str_binary``from_str_octal``from_str_hex`
- Fixed-point numbers can be converted to strings using `Display``Binary``Octal``LowerHex``UpperHex`

# Fixed-point numbers

The [ fixed crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed) provides fixed-point numbers.

- `FixedI8`- `FixedU8`
- `FixedI16`- `FixedU16`
- `FixedI32`- `FixedU32`
- `FixedI64`- `FixedU64`
- `FixedI128`- `FixedU128`

These types can have `Frac` fractional bits, where
0 ≤ `Frac` ≤ n and n is the total number of bits. When
`Frac` = 0, the fixed-point number behaves like an n-bit
integer. When `Frac` = n, the value x lies in the range
−0.5 ≤ x < 0.5 for signed numbers, and in the range
0 ≤ x < 1 for unsigned numbers.

In version 1 the [ typenum crate](https://crates.io/crates/typenum) is used for the fractional bit
count

`Frac`; the plan is to to have a major version 2 with [const generics](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/44580)instead when the Rust compiler support for them is powerful enough.

The main features are

- Representation of fixed-point numbers up to 128 bits wide.
- Conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Comparisons between fixed-point numbers and numeric primitives.
- Parsing from strings in decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Display as decimal, binary, octal and hexadecimal.
- Arithmetic and logic operations.

This crate does *not* provide general analytic functions.

- No algebraic functions are provided, for example no `sqrt`or`pow`.
- No trigonometric functions are provided, for example no `sin`or`cos`.
- No other transcendental functions are provided, for example no
`log`or`exp`.

These functions are not provided because different implementations can have different trade-offs, for example trading some correctness for speed. Implementations can be provided in other crates.

- The *fixed-sqrt*crate

The conversions supported cover the following cases.

- Infallible lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and
numeric primitives are provided using `From``Into`
- Infallible lossy conversions between fixed-point numbers and
numeric primitives are provided using the `LossyFrom``LossyInto`
- Checked lossless conversions between fixed-point numbers and
numeric primitives are provided using the `LosslessTryFrom``LosslessTryInto`
- Checked conversions between fixed-point numbers and numeric
primitives are provided using the `FromFixed``ToFixed``from_num``to_num`[their checked versions](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.checked_from_num).
- Fixed-point numbers can be parsed from decimal strings using

assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
// −8 ≤ I4F12 < 8 with steps of 1/4096 (~0.0002)
let wider_a = I4F12from;
let wider_ans = wider_a / 5 * 17;
let ans2 = I4F4from_num;
// now the answer is the much closer 3 6/16 (~3.4)
assert_eq!;
assert_eq!;
```
The second example shows some precision and conversion issues. The low
precision of `a` means that `a / 5` is 3⁄16 instead of 1⁄5, leading to
an inaccurate result `ans1` = 3 3⁄16 (~3.2). With a higher precision,
we get `wider_a / 5` equal to 819⁄4096, leading to a more accurate
intermediate result `wider_ans` = 3 1635⁄4096. When we convert back to
four fractional bits, we get `ans2` = 3 6⁄16 (~3.4).

Note that we can convert from [ I4F4](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html) to

[using](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[, as the target type has the same number of integer bits and a larger number of fractional bits. Converting from](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[to](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/types/type.I4F12.html)

`I4F12`[cannot use](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/types/type.I4F4.html)

`I4F4`[as we have less fractional bits, so we use](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/convert/trait.From.html)

`From`[instead.](https://docs.rs/fixed/~1.7/fixed/struct.FixedI32.html#method.from_num)

`from_num`## Writing fixed-point constants and values literally

The [ fixed-macro crate](https://crates.io/crates/fixed-macro) provides a convenient macro to write down
fixed-point constants literally in the code.

```
use I16F16;
use fixed;
const NUM1: I16F16 = fixed!;
let num2 = NUM1 + fixed!;
assert_eq!;
```
## Using the *fixed* crate

The *fixed* crate is available on [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/fixed). To use
it in your crate, add it as a dependency inside [ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.7"
```
The *fixed* crate requires rustc version 1.50.0 or later.

## Optional features

The *fixed* crate has these optional feature:

- `serde`, disabled by default. This provides serialization support for the fixed-point types. This feature requires the- *serde*crate
- `std`, disabled by default. This is for features that are not possible under- `no_std`: currently the implementation of the- `Error`- `ParseFixedError`
- `serde-str`, disabled by default. Fixed-point numbers are serialized as strings showing the value when using human-readable formats. This feature requires the- `serde`and the- `std`optional features.- **Warning:**numbers serialized when this feature is enabled cannot be deserialized when this feature is disabled, and vice versa.

To enable features, you can add the dependency like this to
[ Cargo.toml](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/guide/dependencies.html):

```
[]
 = "1.7"
 = ["serde"]
```
## Experimental optional features

It is not considered a breaking change if the following experimental features are removed. The removal of experimental features would however require a minor version bump. Similarly, on a minor version bump, optional dependencies can be updated to an incompatible newer version.

- `num-traits`, disabled by default. This implements some traits from the- *num-traits*crate- *num-traits*crate

## Deprecated optional features

The following optional features are deprecated and may be removed in the next major version of the crate.

- `az`, has no effect. Previously required to enable the cast traits provided by the- *az*crate
- `f16`, has no effect. Previously required to provide conversion to/from- `f16`- `bf16`
